1.text:
What's Real, What's Likely, What's Sci-Fi?

Welcome to the speculative science unit! For the rest of the year, we're heading to the edge of physics, where real data runs into big unknowns. This deck covers dark matter, dark energy and black holes.

Every wild idea we meet will face one question: what's real, what's likely, and what's sci-fi? By the end, you'll be able to judge any wild claim you see online.

2.text:
Proven or Pure Fiction?

Let's start with a challenge. Rank these 5 headlines from proven (1) to pure fiction (5).

Black holes are real, and we have pictures of them. Most of the matter in the universe is invisible. Dark energy is getting weaker over time. Black holes slowly evaporate. You could fly through a wormhole to another galaxy.

Keep your ranking. You will re-rank it in the student task, and you might be surprised which ones move.

3.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Copy these as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can rank claims from proven to fiction and explain why. I can use the Evidence Meter: EF, PH, IS and UK. I can tell what makes a claim scientific. I can explain why fast-spinning galaxies hint at dark matter. I can describe how lensing maps mass we cannot see. I can compare the dark matter suspects. I can weigh dark matter against changing gravity (MOND).

I can explain how supernovae showed the speed-up. I can compare a constant dark energy with a changing one. I can rank the possible endings of the universe. I can split black-hole facts from black-hole guesses. And I can describe how scientists test a wild idea. These connect to NGSS Practice 7 and Indiana standards ES.1.5, ES.1.1, ES.1.2 and ES.1.4, plus some enrichment.

4.text:
The Evidence Meter

This is the tool for the whole unit. Every claim in Decks 21 to 24 gets one of four labels, running from most evidence to least.

ESTABLISHED FACT: tested many ways by many teams. It could still change, but only with big new evidence. For example, the universe is expanding (Deck 19). PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS: testable, with some evidence for it, but not confirmed. Scientists still argue about it. For example, inflation, or the idea that dark energy may change over time.

INFORMED SPECULATION: fits known physics, but has little or no evidence yet. It's often very hard to test today. For example, wormholes you could travel through. UNKNOWN: nobody knows yet, or the evidence is disputed. For example, what dark matter is made of.

Remember, these labels measure evidence, not how cool an idea is.

5.text:
What Makes a Claim Scientific?

A wild idea can still be science, if it passes these three checks.

Testable: it makes a prediction you could check with an observation or experiment. Falsifiable: some result could prove it wrong. If nothing could ever prove it wrong, it is not science. Checked by others: experts review the methods before it is published, and other teams try to repeat it.

All three checks get the label ESTABLISHED FACT, because they're well-documented features of how science works.

Did you know? The idea of falsifiability comes from the philosopher Karl Popper. Try it yourself: could anything ever prove "everything happens for a reason" wrong?

6.text:
Part 1: Dark Matter

Something we cannot see is pulling on everything we can. You first met dark matter in Deck 18. Now we'll look at the evidence more closely, and at the suspects.

Keep one puzzle in mind: how do you weigh something invisible?

7.text:
Galaxies Spin Too Fast

In 1970, Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured how fast Andromeda's stars orbit. Stars far from a galaxy's center orbit about as fast as stars near the center. That's an ESTABLISHED FACT.

If most of the mass were in the bright center, outer stars should orbit slower, just like the outer planets in our Solar System. They don't. The visible stars and gas do not have enough gravity to hold those fast outer stars. ESTABLISHED FACT.

So something extra is pulling: unseen mass, or gravity that works differently. That's an ESTABLISHED FACT too. Which explanation is right? Hold that thought until Slide 11.

8.text:
Mass Bends Light: The Bullet Cluster

Gravitational lensing means mass bends the light from objects behind it, like a giant lens. Einstein's general relativity predicted light bending, and the 1919 solar eclipse measured it. ESTABLISHED FACT.

In the Bullet Cluster, two galaxy clusters collided. Lensing shows most mass is offset from the hot gas. That's a measurement, so it's an ESTABLISHED FACT.

The best explanation is that dark matter passed straight through the crash while the gas slowed down. It's strongly supported, but we still haven't caught a dark matter particle. So it's a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

9.text:
About 5 Times More Dark Matter Than Atoms

Now a third, completely separate line of evidence. The ratio is 27% : 5%, dark matter vs. ordinary matter, as a share of the universe (Planck 2018).

Planck mapped tiny hot and cold spots in the cosmic microwave background (Deck 19). ESTABLISHED FACT. The spot pattern fits best if there is about 5 times (Planck: about 5.4 times) more dark matter than ordinary matter. This amount is measured from gravity, so it's an ESTABLISHED FACT, even though what dark matter is made of is still UNKNOWN.

Dark matter does not give off, absorb or reflect light. We see only its gravity. ESTABLISHED FACT.

10.text:
What Is It? The Suspects

Many teams are hunting. Nobody has caught dark matter yet. Here's the lineup.

WIMPs are heavy particles that almost never touch normal matter. LZ (2024) found no signal in 4.2 tonne-years. Axions are extremely light particles. ADMX and other searches have found no signal yet. Primordial black holes are black holes made in the first second, but many masses are already ruled out. Each suspect is a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Direct detection means a particle hits a detector deep underground. There's been no confirmed hit so far, a null result, and that null result is an ESTABLISHED FACT. What it really is? UNKNOWN.

Did you know? The LZ detector sits about a mile underground in Lead, South Dakota.

11.text:
Or Is Gravity Different?

Same data, two explanations. Option one: dark matter. Unseen mass adds extra gravity. It explains fast-spinning galaxies, the Bullet Cluster offset and the CMB spot pattern. The extra gravity itself is an ESTABLISHED FACT (Slides 7 to 9). The idea that it comes from unseen particles is favored, the leading PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Option two: MOND (Milgrom, 1983). It says gravity changes when pulls are very weak. It fits many galaxy rotation curves well, but it struggles with galaxy clusters and with the Bullet Cluster. It's disfavored, but still a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Good science keeps both ideas on the table until the data decide.

12.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Separate what we saw from what we guess. In the Bullet Cluster, most mass sits away from the hot gas. What does that observation show?

Is it A) something unseen holds most of the mass, B) dark matter is made of WIMPs, C) gravity does not work in clusters, or D) the gas is heavier than everything else? Think about which choice is an observation and which is a hypothesis.

13.text:
Part 2: Dark Energy

Something is making the universe's expansion speed up. In Deck 19 you saw that the universe is expanding. Now comes a big surprise.

If gravity pulls everything together, why is expansion getting faster?

14.text:
The Expansion Is Speeding Up

Let's follow the timeline. In 1929, Hubble showed distant galaxies move away. The universe is expanding. ESTABLISHED FACT. In 1998, two teams found far-away Type Ia supernovae are dimmer than expected. ESTABLISHED FACT. Dimmer means farther, so the expansion has sped up.

In 2011, the Nobel Prize went to Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess for the speed-up. ESTABLISHED FACT. In 2025, DESI mapped 14 million galaxies and found hints that dark energy changes. That's a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

"Dark energy" is the name for whatever causes the speed-up. What it is: UNKNOWN.

15.text:
Constant or Changing?

Dark energy is about 68% of the universe's energy (Planck 2018). That's model-based, but an ESTABLISHED FACT. The question is what kind of dark energy it is.

Option one: a cosmological constant, the same strength everywhere, forever. It's Einstein's "Lambda," and it's been the simplest fit for 25 years. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. Option two: dark energy that changes, with strength changing over time. DESI 2025 found a 2.8 to 4.2 sigma preference for it. But a "discovery" in physics needs 5 sigma, so it's not confirmed. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Sigma measures how unlikely a result is to be a fluke. A 3-sigma result means that if there were no real effect, a result this extreme would show up only about 0.3% of the time. That is NOT the same as a 0.3% chance that the finding is wrong, and plenty of 3-sigma hints have faded away.

16.text:
How Does It All End?

There are three main candidate endings. The Big Freeze: the universe expands forever. Stars burn out. Everything gets cold and dark. It's favored, a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

The Big Rip: dark energy grows stronger and tears apart galaxies, then stars, then atoms. INFORMED SPECULATION. The Big Crunch: the expansion stops and reverses. Everything falls back together. INFORMED SPECULATION.

If DESI's hint holds up, the long-term future gets less certain. That's science changing its mind when new evidence arrives.

17.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Use the Evidence Meter. DESI found a 3-sigma hint that dark energy changes. Which label fits best right now?

Is it A) established fact, B) plausible hypothesis, C) informed speculation, or D) unknown? Look at Slides 4 and 15 to decide, and be ready to say what would move it to a different label.

18.text:
Part 3: Black Holes as Labs

Black holes are where gravity is pushed to its limit. In Deck 17 you learned how massive stars make black holes. Now we'll use them to test physics.

What do we actually know about black holes, and what are we guessing?

19.text:
Seeing the Edge

In 2015, LIGO detected gravitational waves, ripples in space, from two black holes merging. ESTABLISHED FACT. In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope imaged the shadow of M87. In 2022, it imaged Sgr A, at our galaxy's center. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Hawking radiation is the idea that black holes should slowly leak energy (Hawking, 1974). The math is solid, but it has never been observed, because it would be far too faint to detect. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

What happens at the very center, the singularity? UNKNOWN.

20.text:
Wormholes: Shortcut or Sci-Fi?

A wormhole is a tunnel through spacetime that would link two far-apart places. Einstein's equations allow wormhole solutions on paper. ESTABLISHED FACT.

But keeping one open would need "exotic" matter with negative energy (Morris and Thorne, 1988). INFORMED SPECULATION. No wormhole has ever been observed. ESTABLISHED FACT. Whether they can exist in nature at all: UNKNOWN.

A solution on paper isn't the same as a real object.

Did you know? Kip Thorne, one of the wormhole scientists, was the science adviser for the movie Interstellar.

21.text:
How Scientists Test a Wild Idea

This is how scientists test a wild idea, using dark matter as the example. 1, Predict: a dark-matter particle should bump into an atom, very rarely. 2, Build: a detector a mile underground, safe from cosmic rays. 3, Watch: count tiny flashes of light for years. 4, Compare: are there more flashes than the background noise? 5, Repeat: other teams must see the same thing.

LZ did steps 1 to 4 and saw no excess. A null result is still data. ESTABLISHED FACT. Each null result rules out some kinds of WIMP. ESTABLISHED FACT. MOND is tested a different way, with lensing maps of colliding clusters. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Your turn: name a test for "dark energy changes."

22.text:
Student Task: Label 10 Claims

Time to use the Evidence Meter yourself. Make two parts: A, my 10 claim cards, sorted. B, my evidence for each label.

Get 10 claim cards about dark matter, dark energy, black holes and wormholes. Tape each card under EF, PH, IS or UK. For each card, write one piece of evidence, or the evidence that is missing.

Then re-rank your hook headlines from Slide 2. Did any move? Why?

23.text:
Exit Ticket

Show what you learned about judging wild ideas.

First, give one piece of evidence for dark matter. Which label does it earn? Second, why is a null result, like LZ's, still useful? Third, what did the 1998 supernova teams discover? Fourth, label it and explain: "You could travel through a wormhole." Fifth, did your hook ranking change? Which headline moved, and why?

Then look back at your "I can" list from Slide 3 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

24.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards, plus one science practice. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.1.2: describe the expanding universe, or Big Bang Theory, using evidence: the Doppler effect, redshift, Hubble's Law and the cosmic microwave background. ES.1.4: compare the life cycles of low, medium and high mass stars on the H-R diagram, what elements they can make, and whether they become red giants or go supernova.

ES.1.5: show how stars, planetary systems, star clusters, galaxies and galaxy groups fit inside one another, and how big each is. NGSS Science Practice 7: engaging in argument from evidence. Use evidence to defend or reject a claim, and judge how strong the evidence is.
